newsitem.title: USA: U.S. will not join Cargill, N Korea grain deal.
newsitem.headline: U.S. will not join Cargill, N Korea grain deal.

text.p: The U.S. government said on Tuesday it will not get involved in talks between North Korea and grain trader Cargill Inc. to work out financing for food shipments to the famine-stricken nation.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters that despite pressure from Pyongyang, the United States will not interfere in what he called "commercial transactions."

"I think the North Koreans are looking for a more active role by the United States government in these negotiations, but frankly we're not going to get involved," Burns said at a regular news briefing. "We don't get involved in commercial transactions."
A Cargill official also told Reuters on Tuesday that the company views the talks as strictly commercial, and that Washington's help in financing the deal has not been sought.

"We've approached this from the beginning as a commercial deal," said Cargill spokesperson Lori Johnson from the company's headquarters in Minneapolis. "We're still hopeful we can reach a mutually acceptable agreement that will allow us to make a commercial food sale to North Korea."

Cargill, the largest privately held company in the United States and one of the world's biggest grain trading firms, received permission from the Clinton administration early last month to ship 500,000 tonnes of wheat and/or rice to the food-strapped communist nation.

Since then, the company has been trying to arrange the financing of the deal, but the issue appears to have become embroiled in the larger question of more food aid to the struggling country and in plans for U.S. officials to meet with North Korea on proposed peace talks with South Korea.

The diplomatic meetings have been scheduled twice in New York, but have been postponed each time by North Korean officials, who have said that before holding the meeting they want successfully to conclude the grain talks with Cargill.

North Korea has reportedly been trying to put pressure on the U.S. government to help finance the grain deal, hoping that Washington might be more willing to help if it meant the diplomatic talks would proceed.
But no further dates will be set for the talks, Burns said on Tuesday, until the U.S. side is confident that the North Koreans will actually attend the meetings.

"The North Koreans have very important grain negotiations underway, and they prefer to consummate those negotiations before they get onto the meetings with us and the South Koreans in New York," he said. "So we're not going to give out any dates for future meetings until we know that the North Koreans actually intend to attend the meetings."
Burns said that the United States will remain in regular contact with North Korean officials in New York, and that Washington hopes they will agree to come to the briefing.
Cargill officials would not provide any details of the continuing grain negotiations.

The situation has put the powerful but normally low-profile grain company in an unaccustomed media spotlight, and company officials said they are receiving several calls a day from the journalists on the status of the grain talks.
"It's been pretty amazing," said an industry official. Grain transactions are normally worked out in top secrecy, with both parties hoping to attract little, if any attention."
